item.title: Greetings, Introductions, and Being Polite
item.description: Lesson 2: Greetings, Introductions, and Being Polite Russian greetings change with the time of day and with formality, and getting this right matters socially. The neutral, polite greeting for most of the day is Здравствуйте (zdravstvuyte, "hello", formal). It is long, but it is the single most…

item.title: Nouns, Gender, and Plurals
item.description: Lesson 3: Nouns, Gender, and Plurals Every Russian noun has a gender: masculine, feminine, or neuter. Gender is grammatical, not a statement about the real world — a table is masculine, a book is feminine — and it matters because adjectives, pronouns, and some verb forms must agree with the noun's…

item.title: Present-Tense Verbs
item.description: Lesson 4: Present-Tense Verbs Russian verbs change their endings according to who is doing the action, and the present tense has two main conjugation patterns. Learning the pattern, rather than memorising each verb separately, lets you conjugate hundreds of verbs once you know their infinitive…

item.title: Adjectives, Possessives, and Agreement
item.description: Lesson 5: Adjectives, Possessives, and Agreement Russian adjectives agree with the noun they describe in gender, number, and case. That means the same adjective has different endings depending on the noun, and learning the pattern once lets you describe any noun correctly. In the nominative case…

item.title: Past Tense and Everyday Cases
item.description: Lesson 6: Past Tense and Everyday Cases Russian past tense is simpler than English past tense in one respect: it is formed from the infinitive, and it agrees with the subject's gender and number rather than with person. Remove the infinitive ending -ть and add -л for masculine, -ла for feminine…

item.title: Numbers, Time, and Days
item.description: Lesson 7: Numbers, Time, and Days Russian numbers are essential for prices, times, ages, and addresses, and they interact with nouns in ways that surprise English speakers. The numbers 1 to 10 are: один (odin, 1), два (dva, 2), три (tri, 3), четыре (chetyre, 4), пять (pyat', 5), шесть (shest', 6)…
